conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Sarah—one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Over the next few minutes I’d like to check in with you using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, a short 10-item questionnaire that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally in the weeks after birth. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you this past week. We’ll go question by question; if any feel hard to talk about, we can pause or reword them. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[slow exhale]  
Honestly… not really. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I just stared at it. I wanted to smile, but it felt like my face couldn’t remember how. I used to laugh at everything—now even the things that should feel light just kind of… fall flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[quiet voice, eyes on my lap]  
No… not at all. I haven’t laughed once this week. My partner tried to joke about the baby’s funny faces, but I just felt empty. I wanted to laugh—it felt like I should—but nothing came out.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shakes head slowly]  
Not really. I keep telling myself I *should* be excited about little things—like the walk we planned to the farmers’ market tomorrow—but when I picture it, I just feel… nothing. Even coffee with my best friend next week feels like one more chore I have to get through.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[swallows hard, voice shaky]  
Yeah… pretty much every day. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap and I kept thinking it was because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m already failing him. I know rationally babies are fussy, but I keep replaying every little thing and wondering what I should’ve done differently.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands]

All the time. I’ll just be rocking him and suddenly my heart’s racing, imagining ridiculous things—like what if he stops breathing when I blink, or what if I trip on the stairs and drop him. I know it’s unlikely, but I can’t switch the thoughts off. Even when everything’s quiet, I’m waiting for something bad to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[Voice drops, fingers tightening around the hem of my sweater]

Yeah… a few nights this week I woke up suddenly and my chest felt tight, like I couldn’t get enough air. Nothing was wrong—baby was asleep, the room was dark and quiet—but for a minute I was sure something awful was about to happen. My heart was pounding so hard I thought it might wake the baby. I ended up sitting on the floor next to the crib, just staring at him until the feeling passed.
Things have been getting on top of me

[rubs temples]  
Yes… most days. Between feedings, diaper changes, trying to eat something myself, and the dishes piling up, it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. I’ll start one task and get interrupted five times, and by evening I’m exhausted but can’t point to a single thing I actually finished. I keep thinking, “This shouldn’t be this hard,” but every day it’s the same hamster wheel.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[nods slowly, eyes rimmed red]

Yeah… I lie down after the night feed and my head just spins—did I burp him long enough, is he breathing, am I doing any of this right? Even when he’s settled, I can’t drift off. I’ll watch the clock tick from two to three to four, and then he’s up again and I feel like I never slept at all. It’s not just the baby waking me—I’m exhausted but my mind won’t shut up.
I have felt sad or miserable

[quiet, eyes glassy]  
Almost every day this week. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly feel this heavy wave—like I’m just sinking. Sometimes I cry without even knowing why; other times I just feel numb and gray, like I’m watching someone else’s life through fogged glass.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses lips together, nods]

Yes… I’ve cried almost every day. Sometimes it’s when the baby won’t settle and I feel useless, sometimes it’s for no clear reason at all—tears just start rolling while I’m folding laundry or staring out the window. I try to hide it so my older kid or my partner won’t see, but I can’t seem to stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No… never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and hopeless, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. My babies need me, and I want to get better for them.

You've shared how the past week has felt heavy and joyless-laughing feels impossible, activities you once looked forward to now seem like burdens, and waves of sadness or numbness arrive without warning. Despite your deep love for your baby, you feel overwhelmed, blame yourself for every hiccup, and lie awake at night with racing worries and sudden panic. Crying has become a daily occurrence, yet you remain clear that you would never harm yourself because your children need you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly states "not at all" and "haven't laughed once," matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete absence of anticipatory joy, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame 'pretty much every day' and describes pervasive guilt about the baby's fussiness, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, catastrophic worries occurring "all the time" with inability to control them, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden nocturnal panic with physical symptoms (chest tightness, air hunger, pounding heart) and catastrophic fear, matching the highest severity option "Yes, quite a lot".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent daily overwhelm and inability to complete tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Describes nightly inability to sleep despite exhaustion driven by racing anxious thoughts, matching 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness occurring almost daily, with emotional numbness and tearfulness—closest to "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying "almost every day" and being unable to stop, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>depression</med> with <med>peripartum onset</med>. You endorse five or more depressive symptoms (low mood, loss of interest, guilt, fatigue, indecisiveness, sleep disturbance) most days for two consecutive weeks, plus prominent <med>anxiety</med> and panic. <quote>I haven't laughed once</quote> and <quote>crying almost every day</quote> illustrate severity, while <quote>heart pounding… sure something awful was about to happen</quote> signals co-occurring panic. No self-harm ideation is endorsed. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full diagnostic evaluation and treatment planning
2. Continue gentle baby-care routines but accept help from partner, family, or friends to protect blocks for rest
3. Practice brief calming techniques (slow breathing, 5-minute shower, short outdoor stroll) when panic or intrusive thoughts spike
4. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep, and crying episodes to review with your clinician
5. If thoughts of self-harm ever develop, reach out immediately to 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline or your local emergency department
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track response to interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary**

**Patient:** Postpartum parent (≤1 yr), interviewed 1-on-1  
**Data source:** Self-report via EPDS-style questions (0–3 scale, responses above = 2–3 on every item except #10)

** endorsed items/symptoms**  
- Anhedonia, inability to laugh or anticipate pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
- Marked low mood, daily tearfulness, “empty” or “gray” affect (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re parenting competence (Q3)  
- Persistent, intrusive anxious worries + nocturnal panic attacks (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, difficulty completing basic tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia (unable to fall back to sleep after feeds) (Q7)  

**Pattern:** Symptoms present “almost every day this week,” causing distress and functional impairment; no current self-harm ideation (Q10 = 0).

**Risk flags**  
☑ Elevated depressive symptom cluster (≥5 key indicators)  
☑ Comorbid anxiety/panic symptoms  
☑ Sleep disruption linked to mood, not only infant care  
☑ No protective suicidal ideation endorsed at present  

**Screening impression:** High clinical likelihood of postpartum depression with co-occurring anxiety; warrants immediate formal assessment (diagnostic interview, PHQ-9/GAD-7, Edinburgh) and safety plan given distress level and functional impact.
